statement: A 2 by 8 rectangle is to be covered exactly, with no overlaps, by 1 by 2 dominoes and 2 by 2 squares. Any mix of the two pieces may be used, including only one kind. In how many ways can this be done?

choices.misconception: I forgot that the 2 by 2 squares can be used, so I counted only the tilings made of dominoes.
I cut the rectangle into four 2 by 2 blocks, covered each block in 3 ways and multiplied, missing every tiling with a flat domino that crosses from one block into the next.
I lined up my small-case counts against the wrong lengths, so I reported the answer for a 2 by 7 rectangle.
I ran my sequence one step too far, so I reported the answer for a 2 by 9 rectangle.

hints: First count the coverings of a 2 by 1 and a 2 by 2 rectangle.
Look at the left edge of a covering: one upright domino, two flat dominoes stacked, or a 2 by 2 square. Each case leaves a shorter rectangle, so each count comes from the two counts before it.
A 2 by 1 has 1 covering and a 2 by 2 has 3. The count for each new length is the previous count plus twice the one before that.

solutions.reliable: Let T(n) be the number of coverings of a 2 by n rectangle. At the left end there is either one upright domino, leaving 2 by (n - 1), or two flat dominoes stacked, leaving 2 by (n - 2), or one 2 by 2 square, also leaving 2 by (n - 2). So T(n) = T(n - 1) + 2T(n - 2), with T(1) = 1 and T(2) = 3. The sequence runs 1, 3, 5, 11, 21, 43, 85, 171, so T(8) = 171. The transferable idea: when the size is too big to draw, small cases reveal a rule, and the first piece you place tells you why the rule holds.
solutions.elegant: Check the rule on a small case by drawing: a 2 by 3 rectangle has 3 coverings starting with an upright domino and 2 starting with a 2 by 2 block of some kind, so 5 in all, matching 3 + 2 x 1. Then run the rule up to 8.

whyOnTest: Trying small cases first is the 5-point move here: the first piece placed gives a rule, and the near-miss choices come from forgetting a piece or misaligning the sequence by one length.
